newsitem.title: CHINA: China heralds unity offensive in restive region.
newsitem.headline: China heralds unity offensive in restive region.

text.p: The Communist Party chief of China's restive region of Xinjiang has heralded a renewed campaign against separatism with calls for a propaganda offensive and tougher action, state media said.

"We must soberly realise that enemy activities are still very serious," the official Xinjiang Daily quoted regional party secretary Wang Lequan as saying in its July 11 edition, seen in Beijing on Wednesday.

Propaganda and education would be at the heart of the next stage of the campaign to restore social order, which had already seen 17,000 officials sent to reinforce key villages, work units and military farms, Wang told a regional conference.
Xinjiang, a mainly Moslem region in China's remote northwest, has this year been rocked by a string of pro-independence bombings and other violent incidents.
Tough action against violent extremists had already achieved great success, but the war on separatism was a long-term one and there could be no slackening of efforts, Wang said.
"We must... increase the force of our attacks," he said.
Officials should make full use of the July 1 return of the British colony of Hong Kong to Chinese sovereignty in their efforts to boost patriotic loyalties in the region, he said.
"The victorious return of Hong Kong should be used to launch a powerful propaganda offensive," he said.

Every effort should be made to educate the populace about the villainy of those who wanted to split the motherland, he said in a speech that appeared to hint at lingering concerns over the loyalties of some Xinjiang officials.
Regional media last month reported the sacking of 260 grassroots officials, many of whom worked in an area rocked by anti-Chinese riots in February that left nine people dead.
State media have in the past reported that some officials in the region secretly sympathise with separatists, and Wang warned that commitment to national unity was a political prerequisite.
"Under the current situation, officials of all nationalities at all levels must actively stand on the front line against splittism," he said.

Staffing at higher levels in the bureaucracy should be cut to allow more officials to be sent to take part in grassroots work, he said, adding that those working among the masses would receive priority in filling more senior positions.
"From now on, promotions and appointments must be made level by level from the front line," he said.
China's current campaign against Xinjiang separatism is the latest of many aimed at softening anti-Beijing sentiment in the region and at crushing its small, armed independence movement.
Chinese authorities in April executed three people for taking part in the February riots in Xinjiang's Yili district.
In May, eight people were executed after being found guilty of involvement in crimes including the planting of home-made bombs in the regional capital Urumqi that killed nine.
The bombings coincided with the funeral rites in Beijing of paramount leader Deng Xiaoping, who died on February 19.
Tough sanctions should remain an option even as authorities worked to win the hearts and minds of the people, Wang said.
"While all areas should continue face-to-face work to propagandise and educate the masses, at the appropriate time they should turn the focus of the work to striking at the enemy," Wang said.
